title: The Boat of the Three Refuges
summary: The three refuges are made into a boat and the five tathāgatas into its oars; the ocean of existence is crossed as if it were illusion and dream, with the mind as helmsman, and Kāṇha sets out with great bliss as his companion. Munidatta reads the boat as the body of great bliss, the fourth refuge in which body, speech and mind dissolve, and the crossing as made by the means of the fourth joy; in his paraphrase of the last couplet Kāṇha reaches the island of the wheel of great bliss.

flags.note: The Bengali heading names only the rāga. The attribution kṛṣṇā[cārya]pādānām, 'of Kṛṣṇācāryapāda', written before the song, has been removed from line 1a as not part of the verse, and the Tibetan heading (Toh 2293) ends nag po zhabs kyi'o, 'of Kāṇhapāda'. I have not added the poet to the heading; see questions.

lines.gloss: three refuges · boat · made · eight · maidens (read -kumārī with Munidatta; as printed, mārī may be 'having struck')
lines.en: The [three refuges]{trisarana} made into a [boat]{boat}, the [eight maidens]{eight-maidens},

flags.note: Shastri divides aṭhaka mārī. Munidatta cites the words as aṭhakumārī, 'eight maidens' (cp.13.m2), and the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has gzhon nu ma rnams brgyad, 'the eight young women'. I follow them, reading -kumārī for -ka mārī. As printed, aṭhaka mārī could mean 'having struck (or killed) the eight', with mārī from mār-, 'strike, kill'.

The line does not say how the eight maidens relate to the boat: the phrase simply follows 'the three refuges made into a boat'. Crew, passengers or rowers are all possible, so I keep the bare juxtaposition. kia, 'made', is a past participle with no agent expressed.

lines.translit: nia deha karuṇā śūname herī || dhru ||
lines.gloss: own · body · compassion · in emptiness · having seen · (dhru: refrain cue, not translated)

flags.note: The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has rang lus snying rje stong pa'i chung ma can, 'one's own body, having compassion and emptiness for wife'. It seems to divide the same letters as śūna meherī, taking meherī as 'woman, wife' (compare Hindi mehrī), where Shastri divides śūname herī, 'seeing in emptiness'. I follow Shastri. Munidatta's gloss has no word for 'seeing'; it speaks of the unity of emptiness and compassion in one's own body, in the form of coupled union (cp.13.m2), which fits either division.

I take -me as a locative postposition, 'in', governing the pair karuṇā śūna, 'compassion and emptiness' (Munidatta and the Tibetan both treat the two words as a pair), and nia deha, in the direct case, as the object of herī, 'having seen, seeing'. Also possible: 'seeing one's own body as compassion within emptiness'.

lines.translit: tarittā bhavajaladhi jima kari māa suinā
lines.gloss: crossed · ocean of existence · like · having made · illusion · dream
lines.en: The [ocean]{ocean} of [existence]{bhava} was crossed, made like [illusion]{maya} and [dream]{svapna};

flags.note: tarittā is taken as 'crossed', with Munidatta's bhavasamudraṃ kṛṣṇācāryeṇa tīrṇṇaṃ, 'the ocean of existence was crossed by Kṛṣṇācārya' (cp.13.m3). The line names no subject, so I use the passive. The form could instead be an agent noun, 'one who crosses' (compare Sanskrit taritṛ, nominative taritā). The Tibetan (Toh 2293) has srid mtsho las sgrol, 'ferries across from the ocean of existence', in the present. jima kari, 'having made (it) like', is rendered 'made like'.
māa is read as māyā, 'illusion', with Munidatta (māyāmaya, cp.13.m3) and the Tibetan (sgyu ma). The same spelling means 'mother' in song 11.

lines.gloss: middle · braid · waves · known · (dhru: refrain cue, not translated)
lines.en: in the middle, at the [braid]{veni}, the [waves]{wave} were known.

flags.note: The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has dbus su rdzing bcas chu rlabs yong mi shes, 'in the middle, with the pool, the waves are not known at all' (or 'one does not know the waves coming'): a negative the Bengali lacks. Munidatta's gloss is negative too: of the wave, the surging bliss of the self-blessed mind, no self-awareness such as 'I have enjoyed it' is looked for (cp.13.m3). The Bengali would give the negative if divided taraṅga ma muniā, with ma, 'not'. I translate the printed text; with the witnesses the line would be 'in the middle, at the braid, the waves were not known'.

muniā is taken as a past participle of muṇ-, 'know' (Prakrit muṇai); 'knowing the waves' is also possible. beṇī (veṇī) is a braid of hair but also a meeting of streams, as at the Triveṇī of Prayāga; in a crossing the confluence may be meant. I use the glossary's 'braid'. majha beṇī may be 'the middle braid' (Munidatta's madhyaveṇikā) or 'the braid in the middle'. The Tibetan has rdzing, 'pool', for beṇī.

Read in the same construction as 1a (kia, 'made'): the tathāgatas made into oars, as the refuges were made into a boat. The Tibetan (Toh 2293) has de bzhin gshegs pa lnga yis mnyen pa byas, with an instrumental, 'the five tathāgatas did the rowing (or steering)'. keṛuāla may be an oar or a steering paddle.

lines.gloss: row · body · Kāṇha (vocative?) · net of illusion · (dhru: refrain cue, not translated)

flags.note: bāhaa is taken as an imperative, 'row', and kāhnila as a vocative, following Munidatta, who has Kṛṣṇācārya address himself, bho kṛṣṇācāryapādāḥ, with an imperative (cp.13.m4). bāhaa could equally be a present: 'Kāṇha rows the body'. kāhnila is an unusual form of the name (the -ila ending looks verbal). The role of māājāla is unclear: in apposition to the body, as rendered, or what the body is rowed through or away from. The Tibetan (Toh 2293) has kAh+Na lus ni sgyu 'phrul las sgrol byed, 'Kāṇha's body ferries across from illusion'.

Munidatta paraphrases the verb as 'stop' (bādhāṃ kuru), as if hearing bāha- as bādh-, 'obstruct', and makes 'like a net of illusion' describe the ocean of objects, the aggregates, elements and the rest (cp.13.m4); the Tibetan comment agrees (dgag par gyis shig). Elsewhere in the songs bāha- is the verb for rowing a boat, which suits the oars of 3a, so the line keeps 'row'.

lines.gloss: smell · touch (final -ra unexplained; perhaps parasa rasa, 'touch, taste') · as · so
lines.en: Smell and touch, just as they are,

flags.note: parasara is taken as parasa, 'touch' (Sanskrit sparśa; modern Bengali paraś), leaving the final -ra unexplained. Munidatta has 'smell, taste, touch and the rest' (gandharasasparśādi, cp.13.m5) and the Tibetan (Toh 2293) dri reg ro, 'smell, touch, taste', in the Bengali order; both point to a text reading parasa rasa, 'touch, taste', which a scribe could shorten to parasara. As one word it could also be prasara, 'spreading': 'the spreading of scent'. With taste the line would be 'Smell, touch and taste, just as they are'.
jaisom̐ taisom̐, 'as … so', is rendered 'just as they are'. Munidatta has yathaivāsti tathaivāstu, 'as it is, just so let it be' (cp.13.m5); the Tibetan ji lta de lta'o, 'as it is, so it is'.

lines.gloss: sleep · without · dream · like · (dhru: refrain cue, not translated)
mind · helmsman · emptiness · on the māṅga

flags.note: māṅga is kept in source form, as the glossary directs, because its sense is uncertain. Munidatta has naumārga, 'boat-path' (cp.13.m6); the Tibetan (Toh 2293) has grur, 'into the boat'. In song 8 the Tibetan took the word as the stern or prow. The line has no verb; 'as' supplies the link between mind and helmsman.

lines.gloss: set out · Kāṇha · great bliss · in company (as companion) · (dhru: refrain cue, not translated)

flags.note: sāṅge, 'in company', makes great bliss Kāṇha's companion on the way. Munidatta's paraphrase makes great bliss the destination instead: Kṛṣṇācārya went, 'in connection with that' (tatprasaṅgena, perhaps his echo of sāṅge), to the island of the wheel of great bliss (cp.13.m6). The Tibetan (Toh 2293) has zhon nas kAh+Na bde ba chen po'i grogs, 'having boarded, Kāṇha, companion of great bliss', which could make Kāṇha the companion rather than great bliss.

notes.text: Munidatta introduces the song as spoken 'to make firm the meaning already stated', presumably the teaching of the preceding song, which is also Kāṇha's. The Tibetan translation of the comment has 'in order to show the meaning stated' and 'by another song' (glu gzhan gyis).

A [rāga]{raga} is a melodic mode of Indian music; each song's heading names the one it is sung to. The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) calls this one 'dod pa sbyin pa, 'giving what is desired', as if the name were Sanskrit kāmada, and adds nag po zhabs kyi'o, 'of Kāṇhapāda'.

The manuscript writes the attribution kṛṣṇā[cārya]pādānām, 'of Kṛṣṇācāryapāda', before the song; in the edition's text it stood at the head of line 1a, from which it has been removed as not part of the verse. Kṛṣṇācārya is the Sanskrit name of [Kāṇha]{p-kanha}, who names himself in 3b and 5b.

The three refuges are the Buddha, the Dharma and the Saṅgha, in which Buddhists take refuge: the line turns this most basic formula of Buddhist commitment into the boat for the crossing. The song does not say who the eight maidens are or what they do on the boat.

Shastri prints aṭhaka mārī. Munidatta's citation of the words as aṭhakumārī and the Tibetan translation's gzhon nu ma rnams brgyad (Toh 2293) both give 'the eight maidens', which the translation follows. As printed, the words might instead mean 'having struck the eight'.

Munidatta takes 'the three' as [body, speech and mind]{kaya-vak-citta}. The fourth refuge, in which they have dissolved, is the [body of great bliss]{mahasukha-kaya}, and this, he says, is to be understood as the boat in [twilight language]{sandhya-bhasa}. He goes on to the unity of emptiness and compassion in one's own body, in the form of [coupled union]{yuganaddha}, and glosses the eight maidens as the bliss of the Buddha's lordship and the rest, which is experienced.

In Munidatta's comment, 'refuge' after 'fourth' (śara[ṇe]) is partly Shastri's restoration of damaged text. The Tibetan translation of the comment has only 'the fourth' (bzhi pa) there, and its sentence runs differently: 'that mind (yid de) … the fourth, in which it dissolves'.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has 'one's own body, having compassion and emptiness for wife' (rang lus snying rje stong pa'i chung ma can), as if dividing the letters śūna meherī, with meherī 'woman, wife', where Shastri divides śūname herī, 'seeing in emptiness'. The translation follows Shastri.

Illusion (a magician's conjured show) and dream are the stock Mahāyāna comparisons for things that appear without being real. The refrain makes the ocean of existence itself like them, and couplet 4 returns to the dream.

[Braid]{veni} (veṇī) is a plait of hair, and also a place where rivers meet and their currents twist together, as at the Triveṇī of Prayāga. In the middle of a crossing the second sense may be in play: rough water where streams join.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has a negative the Bengali lacks: dbus su rdzing bcas chu rlabs yong mi shes, 'in the middle, with the pool, the waves are not known'. It has rdzing, 'pool', for beṇī, and its version of the comment calls the pool supreme joy in the body. Munidatta's Sanskrit gloss is negative as well. Dividing the Bengali taraṅga ma muniā, with ma 'not', would give the negative; the translation keeps the printed text.

Munidatta says the refrain praises the fourth means: by the boat of the means of the fourth [joy]{ananda}, Kṛṣṇācārya crossed the ocean of existence, having made it illusory and like a dream. In the middle braid, which he calls [supreme joy]{paramananda}, the wave is the surging bliss of the [self-blessed]{svadhisthana} mind, and no self-awareness such as 'I have enjoyed it' is looked for. He supports this with a verse of [Nāgārjuna]{p-nagarjuna} from the [Apratiṣṭhānaprakāśa]{tx-apratisthanaprakasa}: whatever concept arises in the mind is to be given up; the joy that brings supreme bliss is mere conception, and so is dispassion; nirvāṇa is nothing other than the mind free of concepts.
[Tathāgata]{tathagata}, 'thus-gone', is an epithet of a buddha. The tantras arrange their deities in five families, each headed by a tathāgata; the song does not name the five.

The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has de bzhin gshegs pa lnga yis mnyen pa byas, with the tathāgatas as agents: 'the five tathāgatas did the rowing (or steering)'. It uses mnyen pa again in 5a for the Bengali kaṇṇahāra, 'helmsman'.

Munidatta says this couplet, his second verse, teaches the transformation of the [aggregates]{skandha}. One's own body, whose nature is the five purified tathāgatas, is imagined as the oar (kelipāta); taking the boat of [great bliss]{mahasukha}, Kṛṣṇācārya addresses himself: 'O Kṛṣṇācāryapāda, stop the ocean of objects, the aggregates, [elements]{dhatu} and the rest, which is like a net of illusion.' He quotes the [Sūtaka]{tx-sutaka}: aggregates, elements and [senses]{indriya} are each fivefold, and each is blessed by a tathāgata; from what, then, could the acts of saṃsāra arise?

In the Tibetan translation of Munidatta's comment the aggregates are 'completely purified' (phung po yongs su dag pa) where the Sanskrit has pariṇati, 'transformation', and there is no oar: the body is 'to be fully known as equal' (mnyam par yongs su shes par bya). The Sanskrit and the Tibetan comment alike turn the song's rowing into stopping (bādhāṃ kuru; dgag par gyis shig).

The Tibetan line (Toh 2293) has kAh+Na lus ni sgyu 'phrul las sgrol byed, 'Kāṇha's body ferries across from illusion', taking bāhaa as ferrying and māājāla as what one is freed from. Munidatta has Kāṇha addressing himself, so the translation reads kāhnila as a vocative and bāhaa as an imperative; a present, 'Kāṇha rows the body', is also possible.

Parasara is taken as parasa, 'touch' (Sanskrit sparśa). Munidatta lists smell, taste, touch and the rest, and the Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has dri reg ro, 'smell, touch, taste', in the order of the Bengali; both suggest an original parasa rasa, 'touch, taste', shortened in copying. As one word, parasara could also be prasara, 'spreading', of scent.

Munidatta says this couplet, his third verse, teaches the purification of [meditation]{bhavana}, to settle the point beyond doubt. Outer objects, smell, taste, touch and the rest, are to be left just as they are: for one who understands the [true nature]{svarupa} of all things, and is therefore free of sleep and [torpor]{styana}, they appear in the waking state like a dream. He quotes the [Sūtaka]{tx-sutaka}: between sleeping and waking there is no difference of object; one who longs for the fruit of dreams should so conceive it; day and night a creature goes into dream; accomplishment comes with great effort, over a long time.
The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has gnyid ni med kyang rmi lam de bzhin no, 'though there is no sleep, it is like a dream'.

[Māṅga]{manga} is kept in source form because its sense is uncertain. Munidatta renders it naumārga, 'boat-path', in 'the boat-path of emptiness endowed with all supreme aspects'. The Tibetan line (Toh 2293) has grur, 'into the boat', and adds a verb: sems kyis mnyen pas stong nyid grur 'jug la, 'the mind, steering, enters the boat of emptiness'. In song 8 the Tibetan took the word as the boat's stern or prow.

Munidatta says the last couplet, his fourth verse, praises the path: having set the mind as helmsman on the boat-path of [emptiness endowed with all supreme aspects]{sarvakaravaropeta}, Kṛṣṇācārya went by it to the island of the [wheel of great bliss]{mahasukha-cakra}. Where the song has great bliss as Kāṇha's companion, his paraphrase makes it the goal of the crossing; his tatprasaṅgena, 'in connection with that', may render sāṅge. The Tibetan version of the comment has 'the island of great bliss', without 'wheel'.
The Tibetan translation (Toh 2293) has zhon nas kAh+Na bde ba chen po'i grogs, 'having boarded, Kāṇha, companion of great bliss', with zhon, 'mount, board', where the Bengali has calila, 'set out'.

termsOmitted.reason: Only the Tibetan heading names the poet (nag po zhabs kyi'o). The Bengali heading names only the rāga, and the attribution kṛṣṇā[cārya]pādānām was removed from line 1a as not part of the verse. See questions.
Only the Tibetan line has 'boat' (grur), where the Bengali has māṅge; māṅga is kept in source form under its own entry (manga).

proposals.definition: Sleep (Sanskrit nidrā; Old Bengali niṃda; Tibetan gnyid). With dream, a stock comparison for how things appear without being real. Song 13 speaks of a dream without sleep, and Munidatta says one free of sleep and torpor sees things in the waking state as in a dream (cp.13.m5). Distinct from yogic sleep (yoganidrā).
proposals.rationale: Sleep occurs in the song (13.4b) and in Munidatta's comment (cp.13.m5, 'free of sleep and torpor'); sleeping, waking and dreaming recur in the songs and the commentary. A separate entry keeps plain sleep apart from yogic sleep (yoganidra) in song 2. The whole-word pattern keeps নিংদ from matching নিংদা, 'blame'.

questions: Heading: the Bengali heading names only the rāga; the attribution kṛṣṇā[cārya]pādānām was taken out of 1a, and the Tibetan heading names Kāṇha. Should the heading read 'Rāga Kāmoda · Kāṇha' (or '· Kṛṣṇācāryapāda'), as in the style example?
1a: I read aṭhakumārī, 'the eight maidens', with Munidatta and the Tibetan, against Shastri's division aṭhaka mārī (possibly 'having struck the eight'). Confirm?

1b: I keep Shastri's śūname herī, 'seeing … in emptiness'. The Tibetan divides the letters as śūna meherī, 'having compassion and emptiness for wife'. Which should the line follow? And is 'in compassion and emptiness' (with -me governing the pair) right, rather than 'as compassion within emptiness'?

2b: the printed text has no negative ('the waves were known'), but the Tibetan and Munidatta both negate, and dividing taraṅga ma muniā would supply one. Keep the printed sense, or adopt 'the waves were not known'?
2b: the glossary gives 'braid' for veṇī. In a water crossing 'confluence' (a meeting of streams) may be the sense. Keep 'braid' here, or add 'confluence' as a variant?
2a: I put the refrain in the past ('was crossed'), following Munidatta's tīrṇṇaṃ; the Tibetan is present. Past or present?
3b: imperative with vocative, 'row the body, Kāṇha' (Munidatta's grammar), or third person, 'Kāṇha rows the body'? And should 'the net of illusion' stay in apposition to the body?
4a: 'Smell and touch' follows the printed parasara; Munidatta and the Tibetan both list smell, touch and taste (parasa rasa?). Add 'taste'?
5b: the glossary requires 'companion'. Is 'Kāṇha set out with great bliss as companion' acceptable, or would you prefer 'great bliss his companion'?
I propose a new entry, nidra 'sleep', for niṃda (4b) and Munidatta's 'sleep and torpor' (m5), kept apart from yogic sleep. Accept?
